analysis.one_liner: Bans open-air farming of drug- and chemical-producing genetically engineered crops and requires safety testing of genetically engineered foods.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced July 29, 2008 with 7 House sponsors, it was referred to two committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped companies from growing crops genetically engineered to make pharmaceuticals or industrial chemicals outdoors or in common food and feed crops like corn, until a federal tracking system was in place. It would also have required genetically engineered foods to go through formal pre-market safety testing as food additives, with public disclosure of the safety data, civil penalties for violators, and citizen lawsuits to enforce the rules. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers eating genetically engineered foods, since the bill would require safety reviews before marketing and let the public see the underlying data. Farmers, grain handlers, and food companies also benefit indirectly: the bill's own findings say contamination from pharmaceutical crops creates recall costs, export losses, and liability for everyone in the food supply chain [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits growing pharmaceutical or industrial crops in open air or in crops used for human food or animal feed, and imposes a moratorium until USDA final regulations and a tracking system are in effect [S2][S3].

It makes genetically engineered food subject to the food-additive safety process, requiring pre-market petitions, public availability of safety data, specific allergen and toxin testing, and barring additives found likely to be allergenic [S2][S3].

It allows citizens to sue violators or an unresponsive Health and Human Services Secretary, and authorizes civil penalties up to $1,000,000 for pharmaceutical-crop violations and $100,000 per violation for contaminated food [S3].
It gives FDA inspectors authority to detain suspect food and requires all food retailers to register with FDA to speed recalls and seizures [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies developing pharmaceutical and industrial crops (the biotech firms and their farm partners) would bear the cost of a moratorium, confinement requirements, and a tracking system. Biotech food companies would face pre-market testing, petition fees, and public disclosure of their safety data. Food retailers would bear minor registration costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Agricultural biotech firms and their growers

drawbacks.text: The bill's approach treats every genetic construct in food as a food additive, which could mean lengthy petitions, public disclosure of proprietary data, and fees for products already widely marketed, potentially slowing development of genetically engineered crops and increasing costs for food producers [S3].

The bill's findings claim USDA itself acknowledges contamination is 'inevitable' and that its rules aim only to mitigate gene flow rather than prevent it; supporters of the current system argue existing permits and field-trial controls are adequate and that open-air biopharming lowers the cost of producing drugs that might otherwise be unaffordable [S3].

A ban on using common food crops as hosts would push pharmaceutical production to controlled facilities or non-food crops, which the bill directs the National Academy of Sciences to study as alternatives, but critics of such restrictions say the contamination risk is being managed case-by-case rather than warranting a categorical prohibition [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — keeping untested, biologically active drug and industrial chemicals out of the corn and soybean supply — addresses a real contamination risk that the bill's findings say USDA admits it cannot fully prevent. The cost falls on a small biotech sector, though the food-additive requirements could slow food-crop biotech broadly and add compliance costs. The pharmaceutical-crop restrictions are targeted; the food-safety title is the broader and more contested part.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce committees on the day it was introduced, then to subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on July 29, 2008, joined by six Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Grijalva, Lee, Linda Sanchez, DeFazio, Stark, and Hinchey [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee [S5].

On July 29 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and on October 3 to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Specialty Crops, Rural Development, and Foreign Agriculture; no further action was taken [S5].
Neither committee scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural biotech companies and their grower partners are better off: pharmaceutical and industrial crops could keep being grown outdoors under USDA's existing permit system, and genetically engineered foods remained on the market without the bill's pre-market testing and public data disclosure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agricultural biotech firms and pharma-crop growers

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; no vote was ever taken, so party positions beyond sponsorship are not recorded.

industries.industry: Agricultural biotech / pharmaceutical and industrial crop developers
industries.note: The bill would bar open-air cultivation of drug- and chemical-producing crops and ban using common food crops as hosts, halting the outdoor biopharming these companies were conducting under USDA permits. Their argument is that plant-made drugs and chemicals are cheaper to produce, though the bill's findings counter that contamination threatens the food supply [S3].

Foods made with genetically engineered material would become regulated food additives requiring pre-market safety petitions, public disclosure of safety data, allergen testing, and per-violation civil penalties — replacing the current system where such foods reached market without formal pre-market safety testing [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Farmers, grain handlers, and food companies in the conventional supply chain
industries.note: The bill's findings state these businesses face recall costs, export losses, and contamination liability from pharmaceutical crops, and the bill's tracking system and prohibitions aim to prevent such contamination episodes [S3].
Retailers would have to register with FDA to enable faster recalls and seizures — a modest compliance cost in exchange for quicker removal of adulterated food from shelves [S3].
